articles.title: Pavilions as Stances: 6 Unbuilt Proposals from the ArchDaily Community
articles.description: In architecture, the word "pavilion" can describe an endless variety of structures. It might be defined as a principle and a typology, a freestanding structure, a temporary intervention, a gathering place in the city, or a space for experimentation. This last quality is what unites the six unbuilt projects featured here, all designed and submitted by ArchDaily readers. Here, the definition lies in their sculptural qualities and formal exploration, while their permanence and location vary according to each structure's purpose. The proposals also demonstrate another quality inherent to the pavilion: the intention to symbolically represent a stance. Their exploration of form and material thus also reflects a search for a sense of boundary, wonder, or a shared future.

articles.title: Eighth annual Indigenous Peoples' Day powwow
articles.description: On Indigenous Peoples' Day, Monday, Oct. 12 the Center for Diversity & Inclusion's department of Multicultural Affairs hosted its eighth annual powwow celebration inside the Levering Glass Pavilion. A powwow is a traditional social gathering of Indigenous people containing dancing and singing. The event began with remarks from Mary Rose Pedron, the associate director of Multicultural Affairs, and Sherry Ayers, a member of the Lumbee Tribe and former commissioner of the Maryland Commission on Indian Affairs. After the opening, Chief Mark Tayac, the 29th-generation hereditary chief of the Piscataway Nation, took the microphone and directed the rest of the powwow's activities. Chief Tayac began by describing what powwows represent: joy, strength and community. Today, powwows show the world that despite generational trauma, historical oppression and systemic inequality, Indigenous culture has survived and is still thriving. Chief Tayac then called the dancers and drummers to begin the ceremony. A group of four drummers provided the music for most of the dances. The dances were of rotating variety: one was a social dance for anyone to join, one was a solo "Fancy War Dance" performed by one young man, one was a dance performed just by women and one was a couples dance. The routines and costumes were eye-catching and elaborate. In addition to the Native American dance performances, there was also an Indigenous Mexican performance by members of the Mexica people. Their ceremony contained dance, drums and a conch-shell trumpet. Indigenous vendors and community programs set up booths surrounding the middle of the event space. Attendees could purchase jewelry, learn about the resources of the Native American LifeLines Urban Indian Health Program or register for the Baltimore American Indian Center's citywide powwow, taking place on Saturday, Nov. 21. The festivities continued after the dance ceremonies ended, with food being served and people walking around socializing. Aparajita Vaid, a first-year graduate student in the School of Education, described the powwow as a great "opportunity to understand more about [Indigenous] culture." She said the highlight of the event was the ceremonial dances. The School of Public Health's Center for Indigenous Health was also instrumental in setting up the powwow. For anyone wanting to enjoy more indigenous art, the center advertised its upcoming event, Returning to Balance: Indigenous Youth, Arts & Healing, an art and music show taking place both at the Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg Center at 555 Pennsylvania Avenue and virtually on Thursday, Nov. 12.
